1. Sources, scope and how to study

This is the first Artificial Intelligence chapter. It builds the mathematical language needed before search algorithms: what an agent knows, what it can do, how its performance is judged, and what information belongs in a state. Read the lesson before attempting the bank. Solutions are teaching explanations, not an instruction to take a diagnostic test now.

Four written courses were reviewed: Berkeley CS188, Fall 2023, taught by Igor Mordatch and Peyrin Kao, Note 1 by Nikhil Sharma; CMU 15-281, Fall 2023, Vincent Conitzer and Aditi Raghunathan, Introduction and activity solutions; Edinburgh INF2D, written Lectures 1 and 2 in its 2025 material; Stanford CS221, Summer 2012–2013, Chris Piech's Markov Decisions handout. Exact documents, the compared pool, disagreements and reading limits appear in the source audit. The final reference section links each document.

The teaching and problem constructions below are original. They use the reviewed definitions as a starting point, then derive precise conditions and counterexamples. Search-order proofs, Bayesian networks, full MDP algorithms, reinforcement-learning convergence, game equilibria and learning theory have their own later chapters. Here they appear only where necessary to make agent foundations mathematically meaningful. A finite scope and checked derivations support reliable study; they cannot certify performance on every possible unseen question.

2. The agent–environment boundary

An agent receives observations and chooses actions. Its environment is the part of the model outside that decision mechanism. A physical robot can have cameras and motors; a software agent can receive a message and send a database request. “Sensor” and “actuator” name these information and influence channels, not necessarily physical devices. A stored image is an observation. A command to move is an action. The resulting displacement is an environmental outcome, which can differ from the command.

Use a discrete decision index t. Write st for the environment state, ot for the observation, and at for the selected action. In a deterministic model, an observation map O and transition map T give

ot=O(st),at=f(o0,…,ot),st+1=T(st,at).

The order matters: the action selected from the current observation affects the next state, not the already received observation. In a stochastic model, T(s,a,s') denotes a conditional probability rather than a successor state. Never use the same symbol as both a state and a probability without specifying the convention.

The boundary is a modelling choice. A robot team controlled by one central planner can be one decision maker with a joint action. An opponent with separate objectives must still be represented in that team's environment. Counting bodies is not the same as identifying independent decision makers. Include external processes only to the detail needed for prediction and evaluation.

Percept, internal update, action and next state

The selected action affects the next physical state; the percept already received is not rewritten.

Memory describes the world but is not itself the physical world.

3. Agent function, program and architecture

An agent function specifies behaviour for every possible finite observation history. If P is the percept alphabet and A the action set, one conventional signature is f:P*→A. If no action is selected before the first percept, restrict the domain to nonempty histories. A program is a finite implementation of such behaviour on an architecture, which supplies memory, computation and sensor/actuator interfaces. Different programs can implement the same function; a particular function need not be implementable within a specified memory or time budget.

A table of actions for histories is a behavioural description, not a scalable design. Suppose there are p percepts and a actions and the agent makes decisions after histories of lengths 1 through H. The number of table entries is

NH=∑t=1Hpt.

For p≠1, multiply the sum by p and subtract the original to obtain NH=(pH+1−p)/(p−1). For p=1, it is H. Each entry independently selects one of a actions, so the number of unrestricted tables is aNH. With p=2,a=3,H=3, there are 2+4+8=14 entries and 314 functions. A memoryless percept rule needs only p entries and has ap possibilities.

This counts all syntactic histories, including some unreachable in a fixed environment. Behavioural equivalence on reachable histories can identify different tables. A deterministic agent's own previous actions can be reconstructed from its known function and percept history. For a randomized agent, actions or its random-state information may need to be included explicitly; use the richer history ht=(o0,a0,o1,…,at−1,ot) when that distinction matters.

4. Performance measures, rewards and PEAS

PEAS describes Performance measure, Environment, Actuators, Sensors. It is a specification of the task, not a four-step search algorithm. A performance measure evaluates what happened. A reward is a numerical feedback signal used inside a model or learning procedure. They may agree, but equality must be designed rather than assumed.

For a delivery robot, a complete specification might evaluate completed deliveries, lateness, energy consumption and collisions over a stated horizon; include corridors, doors and other traffic in the environment; provide drive, stop and load commands as actuators; and provide localisation, obstacle range, battery and package sensors. “Be efficient” is not a usable performance measure until its tradeoffs and units are defined.

One possible score is J=10D−2L−E−100C, where D is deliveries, L is late minutes, E is energy units and C is collisions. Compare two runs explicitly. Run A has (D,L,E,C)=(3,2,4,0), giving 22. Run B has (4,0,3,1), giving −63. Under this score, more deliveries do not justify a collision. If collisions are forbidden rather than merely expensive, remove unsafe policies from the feasible set; a finite penalty is not automatically a hard constraint.

A badly chosen proxy can reward the wrong behaviour. Paying for each “clean” message lets an agent repeatedly announce cleanliness without cleaning. Paying for dirt removed can encourage re-dirtying if that is allowed and unpenalized. Define the desired outcome independently of the agent's self-report, include all allowed actions, and test what maximizes the proposed score.

5. Rationality is conditional, not omniscience

An action is rational when it maximizes expected performance given the agent's information, model, available actions and evaluation criterion. The expectation concerns possible outcomes, not only the outcome later observed. A rational decision can have an unfortunate realization. An omniscient decision maker knows the actual future consequence; ordinary rationality grants no such knowledge.

For a finite one-step model, let b(s∣h) be the current belief and let U(s,a) include all action-dependent consequences and costs. Then

EU(a∣h)=∑sb(s∣h)U(s,a),a*(h)∈argmaxa∈A(h)EU(a∣h).

The maximizing set can contain several actions. A deterministic tie rule chooses one; randomized mixing among tied maximizers remains optimal. An empty legal action set requires an explicit termination or failure convention, not an undefined maximum.

For example, a safe action pays 4 for certain. A risky action pays 10 with probability 3/5 and −2 otherwise. Its expected payoff is 6−4/5=26/5>4. Choosing it maximizes expected payoff, although a realized payoff of −2 is possible. If the stated utility is not money, calculate the expected utility of outcomes rather than applying utility to the expected money. Model error and mistaken preferences can make an internally consistent maximizer perform poorly under the true task measure; always state which model is being used.

A lower realized result does not retrospectively alter the available-information optimum.

6. Deriving decision thresholds

Many agent questions reduce to comparing two affine functions of a probability. Suppose hidden state H has probability p, and L has probability 1−p. Actions A and B have utilities (uAH,uAL) and (uBH,uBL). Subtract their expected utilities:

EU(A)−EU(B)=p(uAH−uBH)+(1−p)(uAL−uBL).

If the coefficient of p is positive, solve the resulting inequality with its direction unchanged; if negative, reverse it; if zero, the decision is constant or tied. Intersect the answer with 0≤p≤1. A threshold outside this interval means one action is preferred throughout the feasible range.

Take A with utilities (12,−4) and B with (5,5). Then EU(A)=16p−4, and A is optimal exactly when p≥9/16, with a tie at equality. The statement “choose A if H is more likely” is false: p=0.53 exceeds one half but is below 9/16. A prior change, sensor result or loss asymmetry can cross the actual threshold.

An action is statewise dominated if another action has at least as much utility in every state and strictly more in at least one. Weak dominance guarantees no lower expectation; strict expected improvement additionally requires positive probability on a state with strict improvement. Do not delete a tied action by silently assuming every state has positive probability.

7. Utility scales, risk and robust decisions

For a common outcome distribution, the transformation U'=αU+β with α>0 preserves expected-utility rankings because E[U']=αE[U]+β. A negative scale reverses rankings; a zero scale makes all outcomes equal. An arbitrary increasing transformation preserves rankings of individual certain outcomes, but need not preserve rankings of lotteries.

Let lottery A pay 0 or 100, each with probability one half; B pays 40 certainly. Expected money favours A, 50>40. With utility u(x)=x for nonnegative money, expected utility favours B because 5<40. Risk preference is encoded by utility; choosing a smaller expected monetary amount is not automatically irrational.

When no probability model is supplied, expected utility cannot be numerically determined from the payoff table alone. A worst-case rule chooses the action maximizing its minimum payoff. A minimax-regret rule first subtracts each action's payoff from the best available payoff separately in each state, then minimizes the largest regret. These are different criteria, not interchangeable definitions of rationality. With A= (8,−2) and B= (3,3), maximin chooses B; under prior p=4/5, expected utility chooses A because 6>3.

8. Observability and the information actually available

Full observability means the current percept determines all decision-relevant state information in the declared model. It does not mean the agent knows future random outcomes, transition parameters or other agents' future choices. Partial observability means distinct relevant states can produce the same percept. A noisy camera is one cause; an exact local sensor in a larger world is another.

With deterministic observations, define the observation class [s]O={s':O(s')=O(s)}. An observation is sufficient to identify state if these classes are singletons over the relevant reachable states. It can still be sufficient to choose an optimal action when a class has several states but all share a maximizer. This is why partial observability alone does not prove that memory is beneficial.

Consider two hidden conditions requiring the same safe action. Their sensor readings can be identical without reducing decision quality. Conversely, if the same reading occurs after two histories whose unique optimal actions differ, every deterministic memoryless rule fails on at least one of those histories. The failure is informational: a rule cannot output two different actions for the same input.

Both histories end with the same sensor symbol, but the uniquely correct actions differ.

Store a key bit or obtain another observation; changing the rule alone cannot recover omitted information.

9. Deterministic, stochastic and strategic environments

A deterministic transition gives one successor for each fully specified state and action. A stochastic transition supplies a distribution. Unknown dynamics concern the agent's knowledge of the transition, not whether the transition is deterministic. A fair die is stochastic even if its distribution is known. A fixed but initially unknown door code can be deterministic and unknown.

Hidden deterministic state can make observations appear random. If the true state includes a hidden bit z and the next observation is z, uncertainty about z induces a distribution over observations despite deterministic physical evolution. Augmenting the state can reveal determinism; adding irrelevant variables does not necessarily help the agent observe them.

In a strategic environment, other decision makers choose actions according to their objectives. Their behaviour may be predictable or randomized, but replacing them with a fixed random generator is an additional modelling assumption. A game may have a deterministic next board given the joint action while a single player's future remains uncertain. Determinism and number of agents are separate axes.

10. Episodic, sequential and time-dependent tasks

An episodic task separates decisions into episodes whose consequences do not affect later opportunities or performance. A one-letter classification task can be episodic when labels are independent and each decision has its own loss. A mail robot with a shared battery or a daily quota is sequential: today's action changes tomorrow's resources. Independent observations alone do not establish episodicity.

A static environment does not evolve during the agent's deliberation in the chosen decision model. It can change when the agent executes an action. A sliding puzzle is a simple example. In a dynamic environment, traffic or other processes move while the agent thinks. In a semidynamic task, the physical state can remain fixed while performance changes with elapsed time, as in a timed puzzle. If time changes action feasibility, augment the state with time and describe the resulting model explicitly.

Discrete and continuous refer separately to states, observations, actions and time. Integer room numbers do not make continuous steering commands discrete. A countably infinite counter is discrete but not finite. A sampled model of a continuous system is an abstraction; it does not make the underlying physics discrete.

11. Classify a task by justified assumptions

For an untimed, fully displayed deterministic board puzzle with one player, a known move rule and no external changes, the usual classification is fully observable, deterministic, sequential, static, discrete, known and single-agent. Change one assumption at a time. Hide a tile and observability changes; add a clock penalty and it becomes semidynamic; let a tile slip randomly and the transition becomes stochastic; withhold the slip probability and model knowledge becomes incomplete as well.

Do not classify “chess”, “driving” or “a robot” by a memorized word alone. Standard chess has no hidden pieces, but board arrangement without castling rights, side to move, en-passant rights and relevant draw history is not a complete rule state. Timed chess adds an elapsed-time issue. Driving models depend on sensor limitations, other road users, actuation uncertainty and the time resolution chosen.

For each axis, write a witness: two indistinguishable states for partial observability; two positive-probability successors for stochasticity; a resource changed by an action for sequentiality; an exogenous change during thought for dynamic behaviour. A witness is more reliable than a label unsupported by the task statement.

12. Simple reflex and model-based reflex agents

A simple reflex policy maps the current percept to an action. A condition–action implementation can test several fields in that percept; it is not restricted to one Boolean condition. Such a policy may be optimal for a suitable task, including a sequential one if the percept already supplies sufficient state and the optimal action is compiled into a rule.

A model-based reflex agent maintains an internal summary mt and updates it using the previous action and new percept:

mt=F(mt−1,at−1,ot),at=π(mt).

The summary may be a room map, a finite controller state, a set of possible states or a probability distribution. “Model-based” concerns representing how observations and actions relate to the world. “Reflex” concerns applying a current condition–action rule rather than explicitly searching over future consequences at decision time. An agent can have memory without performing online planning.

Using a stale summary is a common implementation error. First predict the effect of the previous action, then incorporate the current observation, then choose a new action. If cleaning may fail, recording “clean” after issuing the command is unjustified unless the new percept verifies it or the model assigns certainty to success.

For the reliable, no-recurrence two-room model, the following controller shows the difference between a current percept and persistent memory. Each cleanliness entry initially means unknown, rather than falsely assuming that an unobserved room is clean. An observation of dirty replaces any earlier clean report. The update is justified only by the reliable sensor and no-recurrence model.

# Persistent fields survive between calls.
verified_clean = {"L": False, "R": False}

def choose_action(position, dirty):
    verified_clean[position] = not dirty
    if dirty:
        return "Clean"  # Verify the result on the next call.
    if all(verified_clean.values()):
        return "Stop"
    return "Right" if position == "L" else "Left"

This controller does not claim that an issued Clean command has already succeeded. It waits for the next observation. Starting with both rooms dirty, successive percepts lead to Clean, Right, Clean, Stop. With dirt recurrence, the persistent bit for a room not currently observed can become stale, so the code is not a guaranteed maintenance policy for that different model.

13. Goal-based and utility-based choice

A goal is a condition on states or histories. Goal-based reasoning seeks a way to satisfy it. Several conditions can form a conjunction: deliver both parcels and return to the charger. Utility grades outcomes and can prefer one goal-reaching run over another because it is faster, safer or less costly. Goals alone do not determine those preferences unless costs or an ordering are separately specified.

These architecture labels are not a strict hierarchy of intelligence. A compiled policy can execute the exact action previously found by a planner. A utility maximizer can use a learned model. A model-based reflex controller can outperform a slow planner under a short deadline. The question is which representation, computation and objective fit the task.

Achievement means reaching a target at some time. Maintenance means avoiding a forbidden condition throughout the relevant run. “Eventually arrive” and “never collide” are not the same goal. A run that collides first and arrives later satisfies the former but violates the latter. A terminal goal test alone cannot detect a past collision unless that information is retained in the state or evaluated over the trajectory.

14. Learning, exploration and bounded computation

A learning agent changes its behaviour or model using experience. A performance element chooses actions; a critic supplies task-related feedback; a learning element updates the performance element; an exploration mechanism can select informative experiences. This functional decomposition does not require four physical processors or four independent programs.

Learning can improve the sensor model, transition model, utility estimate, rules, action-value estimates or a direct policy. The useful method depends on the target, prior knowledge, available data and feedback. Data quantity alone cannot determine it. A deterministic environment can require learning an unknown map. A stochastic environment with a fully known model need not require model learning.

Exploration can be rational because it improves later decisions, but it is not obligatory in every unknown environment. Suppose testing an unknown door yields information worth at most 2 in all remaining decisions and costs 5 now. The test is not justified by information value. With no remaining decisions and no immediate benefit, learning for its own sake is not required by the specified performance measure.

Bounded optimality compares implementable programs on a specified architecture, accounting for time and resources. If a fast decision has expected utility 8 and computation raises decision quality to 10 but costs 3, the fast choice has larger net utility. “More reasoning” needs a value calculation; it is not a universal improvement.

15. Sufficient state and the Markov property

A state is sufficient for prediction if, conditioned on it and the selected action, earlier history adds no relevant information about the next state and reward. In a finite controlled model, write

P(st+1,rt∣ht,at)=P(st+1,rt∣st,at).

This is a property of the representation and model, not a guarantee supplied by calling a variable “state”. Position alone is insufficient if a locked door depends on whether a key was collected. Add a key bit. Position alone is insufficient if future cost depends on remaining fuel. Add fuel. Finite-horizon optimal policies can depend on the remaining time even when physical transitions are stationary; either retain a time-indexed policy or include time in state.

Full history is often a formally sufficient representation, but grows without bound. Seek a compact sufficient summary. A summary sufficient for one objective need not be sufficient for another. For reaching a fixed room, collected food may be irrelevant; for collecting every item, remaining-item bits are essential. State variables are selected relative to transition, legality, goals and costs together.

16. The exact criterion for a rational memoryless policy

Fix a finite action set and a set of relevant histories. For each history h, let M(h) be the set of actions optimal under the specified continuation criterion. A deterministic policy using only current percept o can be optimal at every relevant history if and only if

⋂h:last(h)=oM(h)≠∅for every occurring percept o.

Necessity. A memoryless rule selects one action π(o). If it is optimal at every history with percept o, that same action belongs to every corresponding M(h), hence to their intersection.

Sufficiency. Choose one action from each nonempty intersection and define π(o) to be that action. By construction it is optimal at every history sharing that percept. The argument assumes the relevant optimal-action sets have already been defined consistently; it does not compute them from nothing.

For two histories with M(h1)={A,B} and M(h2)={B,C}, B works even though state is uncertain. With M(h1)={A} and M(h2)={B}, no current-percept-only rule works. Distinguishing those histories requires at least two internal conditions. Randomization does not restore optimality at both when each has a different unique maximizer: any mixture assigning positive mass to the wrong action loses utility at one history.

17. Beliefs: sets and probability distributions

When the world is partially observed, an agent can maintain a belief set of states compatible with the history. Under deterministic dynamics, first propagate every possible current state through the chosen action, then discard successors incompatible with the new observation. If Bt is the current set,

Bt+1={T(s,at):s∈Bt,O(T(s,at))=ot+1}.

For nondeterministic dynamics, replace each singleton successor with its permitted successor set. An empty belief indicates inconsistent observations or a model error, unless the history was assigned probability zero by design. It is not a proof that the physical world has no state.

A probability belief also weights compatible states. For transition probabilities T and observation likelihood Z(o∣s',a), predict and condition:

b^(s')=∑sT(s,a,s')b(s),b'(s')=Z(o∣s',a)b^(s')∑xZ(o∣x,a)b^(x).

The denominator must be positive. At zero, do not divide by zero or return a fabricated uniform posterior; report that the observation is impossible under the current model. Set propagation and probability filtering answer different questions. Two beliefs with identical support can select different optimal actions because their weights differ.

18. A complete binary-sensor calculation

Let hidden state H have prior 3/10. A positive sensor result occurs with probability 4/5 in H and 1/5 in L. Then

P(+)=31045+71015=1950,P(H∣+)=1219.

A negative result has probability 31/50 and posterior P(H∣−)=3/31. Both branches must be considered before purchasing the sensor. The posterior is not the sensor's accuracy: 12/19 differs from 4/5 because the prior matters.

Use the earlier actions A= (12,−4) and B= (5,5). Before sensing, A has utility 4/5 and B has 5, so B wins. After a positive result, A has 116/19>5. After a negative result, A has −76/31<5, so B wins. Expected optimized utility after the free signal is

195011619+31505=27150.

The expected value of sample information is 271/50−5=21/50. A sensor cost of 1/4 leaves net gain 17/100, so acquiring it is rational in this one-step model; cost 1/2 makes the net gain negative. The editable laboratory recalculates every branch exactly, including ties and zero-probability observations.

19. Why free information cannot hurt under stated conditions

Let Y be a signal available before action, with no effect on the environment, no delay, no cost and no restriction forcing the agent to use it. For each signal value, let EU(a∣Y) be conditional utility. If a0 is optimal before sensing, then for every possible signal,

maxaEU(a∣Y)≥EU(a0∣Y).

Average over the signal and apply total expectation. The expected optimized value after information is at least EU(a0), the best prior value. This proves nonnegative information value under the stated conditions. It can be zero: if one action remains best after every signal, the information does not change the decision.

Perfect information reveals the hidden state. Its value is an upper bound on the value of a less informative signal in the same one-step model, because a perfectly informed decision maker can simulate the signal and follow its policy. For A= (12,−4), B= (5,5) and prior 3/10, perfect information yields (3/10)12+(7/10)5=71/10, so its value is 21/10, exceeding 21/50 for the noisy sensor. Costs, delay, forced disclosure or an imperfect optimizer invalidate the simple “cannot hurt” conclusion if included in performance.

20. A fully specified two-room vacuum world

Represent a physical state by (x,dL,dR), where x∈{L,R} and each dirt bit is zero or one. There are 2·22=8 states. The local percept (x,dx) has only four values and does not reveal the other room's dirt. The dynamics below are deterministic and known: Left sets position to L, Right sets it to R, Clean sets the current dirt bit to zero, and Stop leaves the state unchanged. Dirt never reappears. No clock or external process changes the state while the agent deliberates.

The goal is both dirt bits zero. With unit action costs, a known state (L,1,1) has a three-action solution Clean, Right, Clean. Fewer than three actions are impossible: two distinct dirty rooms require two cleans, and reaching the second room requires a move. With no sensors and an arbitrary initial physical state, Right, Clean, Left, Clean guarantees the goal in four actions. Right deliberately merges the two possible initial locations; cleaning then reduces uncertainty about dirt. Sensorless planning can succeed without discovering the exact initial state.

A local rule “clean if dirty; otherwise go to the other room” cleans both rooms but then moves forever. If movement is penalized after the goal, that infinite loop is wasteful. A model-based controller can remember verified cleanliness of both rooms and stop. If dirt can recur, the stop rule requires revision; the proof used the no-reappearance assumption.

21. Formulating a deterministic search problem

A search problem specifies a state set S, initial state s0, legal action set A(s), result function T(s,a), goal test G(s) and step cost c(s,a,s'). A solution is a legal action sequence reaching a goal. An optimal solution minimizes the declared path cost, which for additive costs is

g=∑t=0k−1c(st,at,st+1).

The goal test need not list all goal states explicitly. “No remaining dirt” is an implicit predicate on two bits. Distinguish a zero-length solution when the initial state is already a goal from failure when no solution exists. Failure is not an empty plan unless the API explicitly distinguishes those cases.

Path cost and depth agree only with equal positive action costs, up to a constant factor. A route with two edges of cost 100 is more expensive than a route with three edges of cost 1. Negative-cost cycles can destroy existence of a minimum-cost solution; zero-cost cycles can create infinitely many equal-cost paths. Algorithms and their guarantees must state the relevant cost assumptions. The next chapter treats uninformed search; this chapter establishes the model it operates on.

22. Safe abstraction and omitted variables

Let φ map detailed states to abstract states. A useful exact deterministic abstraction requires equivalent detailed states to agree on goal status and legal abstract actions. For every common action, their successors must remain equivalent and their corresponding costs must agree:

φ(s)=φ(t)⟹φ(T(s,a))=φ(T(t,a)).

Together with matching legality, goals and costs, this makes the abstract transition well-defined. Induct on action-sequence length: the base states have the same abstraction; one legal action preserves equivalence by the displayed condition; repeat. The two concrete executions then produce matching abstract states, accumulated costs and goal results. This proves exact preservation for the specified action sequences. A looser relaxation used to obtain a lower bound need not satisfy these exact conditions; it has a different purpose.

If two states share a room position but differ in possession of a required key, “position only” merges a state where Open is legal with one where it is illegal. The abstract plan can become unrealizable. If fuel differs, a common move may be feasible in only one state. If the objective penalizes a previous collision, add a flag or keep a history-based evaluator. The correct abstraction removes irrelevant detail, not inconvenient constraints.

A key bit repairs an invalid state abstraction

At the same position X, Open has different legality depending on key possession.

A missing key is a missing precondition, not a different arrow label on the same exact abstract edge.

23. Count states by independence and constraints

Apply the product rule only when choices are independently allowed. A robot in one of n rooms with n independent dirt bits has n2n syntactic physical states. If exactly k rooms are dirty, it has n(nk) states. If the robot must be in a clean room, choose its location first and assign dirt only to the remaining rooms, obtaining n2n−1.

For two labelled robots in distinct rooms, positions number n(n−1), not n2. If robots are indistinguishable and all dynamics and objectives are symmetric, unordered positions number (n2). Removing labels is invalid if the robots have different capacities or actions. A state-space product is an upper bound when some combinations are unreachable; distinguish legal configuration count from reachability from a particular start.

With N physical states, there are 2N belief subsets, including the empty set; there are 2N−1 nonempty subsets. The belief states reachable under a particular sensor and transition model can be far fewer. Probability distributions over just two physical states already form a continuum, even though the support-set space is finite.

24. State graphs, search nodes and contingent policies

A state graph has one vertex per model state and edges for legal transitions. A search-tree node records a particular path prefix: state, parent, generating action and accumulated cost. Different nodes can contain the same state. A cycle can make a search tree infinite while the state graph is finite. Recognizing equal states requires a sufficient state representation; merging two nodes by position alone is unsafe if one has a key and the other does not.

Under deterministic, known transitions and a known initial state, an action sequence can predict the entire run. Under observation-dependent uncertainty, a contingent policy can select different actions after different observations. A fixed sequence is a special case of a policy. There need not be a fixed sequence as good as the best contingent policy, but uncertainty does not logically require a contingent solution in every task; the sensorless vacuum sequence is a counterexample.

For a known current state with two available actions and three possible observations before a second action, a full two-step contingent policy selects the first action and one second action for each observation. If all combinations are allowed, there are 2·23=16 such policies. There are only 22=4 fixed sequences. If observations are impossible on some branches, count reachable decisions separately.

Different paths produce different search nodes

Two paths can end at the same goal state but have different parent records and costs.

Goal state equality does not imply equal search-node path cost.

2<3,200>3

A self-loop generates infinitely many prefixes

There are two states but a distinct goal path for every number of self-loop repetitions.

The search node remembers a path prefix; the physical vertex X is the same after every loop.

d=k+1

An inductive winning policy executed on actual counters

Normal play: remove one or two; the player taking the last wins. Agent leaves multiples of three.

The exact count is discrete; removed counters fade rather than pretending to split continuously.

25. Sequential returns and evaluation

For a finite horizon H, a common return is G=∑t=0H−1γtrt, optionally followed by a terminal utility with its specified discount. With γ=1, rewards add without discounting. With 0<γ<1, earlier rewards have greater weight. For bounded rewards |rt|≤R and an infinite horizon, the geometric series gives |G|≤R/(1−γ). Without a bound or discount, existence of an expected return needs separate justification.

A greedy action maximizing immediate reward can be poor for a sequential objective. Action A pays 6 now and −10 next; B pays 1 now and 8 next. With γ=1, their returns are −4 and 9. With general γ, A is preferred only if 6−10γ≥1+8γ, or γ≤5/18. The ranking depends on the stated horizon and discount, not a slogan about greed.

Evaluation compares policies on the same model distribution and task criterion. One successful run does not prove rationality; one unlucky run does not disprove it. An independently derived answer is not an official examination key. A simulator that verifies its finite transitions does not prove a claim about every environment. These distinctions keep empirical checks and mathematical guarantees separate.

26. Summary and examination workflow

Start by identifying the objective, information, actions and model. Separate a percept from a physical state and separate a physical state from an internal summary. When classifying an environment, give the assumption or witness for each axis. When deciding an action, write its utility in every relevant state, weight by the correct belief, include costs, and compare the resulting values. Solve ties and boundaries explicitly.

When formulating a problem, ensure that states retain everything needed for action legality, transition, goal and cost. Count independent choices and then remove forbidden combinations. Distinguish full configuration space from reachable states, physical states from belief states, and state vertices from search nodes. For information acquisition, optimize separately after each possible signal before averaging; optimizing after averaging answers a different question.

When an assertion says “always”, try a minimal counterexample: a partially observed task with one common best action; a deterministic unknown map; a static puzzle changed by the agent's own moves; a free signal that never changes the best action; a costly computation whose quality gain is too small; or a sequential task whose sufficient percept makes a compiled reflex policy optimal. The detailed rules below attach the necessary conditions to each conclusion.

27. Worked mathematical and conceptual problems

The original bank develops counting, information, rationality, architecture and exact modelling from medium calculations to hard synthesis. Course reconstructions have their own provenance labels and independently written data or qualifications. The authentic items are checked English adaptations of the original PDF page, with the original option order retained. Two directly relevant MSc items are included; the inspected recent PhD CE pages did not supply a matching foundations item, and no unrelated question is relabelled as agent foundations. All answers are independently derived.

Authentic examinations: task environment and agent learning

Question 1. Agent performance depends on its task environment

Authentic examination · checked English adaptation

MSc CE 1405 · Q71 · PDF page 15. Independently derived answer; not an official key.

How well an agent can behave depends on which factor?

1.

The agent designer.

2.

The agent sensors.

3.

The nature of the environment.

4.

The agent actuators.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Correct option: 3.

The intended best answer is option 3: the task environment determines which behaviour and information can achieve the performance criterion. Sensors and actuators are important components of the agent, but their adequacy is judged relative to that environment and task. A local dirt sensor can suffice for one cleaning objective and be insufficient for another requiring exact global dirt information. The designer is not a mathematical property of the task. The short original wording should not be strengthened into a claim that sensor and actuator quality never matter: rationality is evaluated relative to the information, action capabilities and performance criterion available in the specified environment. This is a conceptual best-choice item, not an exclusivity theorem.

Question 2. Learning-method selection is not determined only by data quantity

Authentic examination · checked English adaptation

MSc CE 1405 · Q75 · PDF page 15. Independently derived answer; not an official key.

Any part of an agent program can be improved using machine learning. The kind of improvement and the methods used to make it do NOT depend on which of the following?

1.

The prior knowledge available to the agent.

2.

It depends only on the amount of available data.

3.

Which part of the agent is to be improved.

4.

The data available and the feedback received about those data.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Correct option: 2.

Option 2 is the intended incorrect dependency statement. The word only is decisive: data quantity cannot by itself determine the type of improvement or learning method. Prior knowledge can justify a model structure or constrain hypotheses. The target component determines whether the output is a sensor model, transition distribution, utility estimate or direct policy. Available data and feedback distinguish, for example, labelled examples from reward-only interaction. Two tasks with the same number of observations can require very different methods when one supplies labels and the other supplies only delayed rewards. Options 1, 3 and 4 are genuine considerations; they need not each influence every possible special case to be relevant dependencies in general.

Original and reconstructed mathematical/conceptual problems

Question 1. Percept histories are not physical states

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical problem

An agent has three possible percepts and two possible actions. It acts after each history of length one or two. Count unrestricted deterministic agent functions and memoryless percept policies. Explain the difference.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

There are 3 histories of length one and 32=9 of length two, so a full table has 12 independent entries. Each entry selects one of two actions, giving 212=4096 tables. A memoryless policy assigns one action to each of three current percepts, giving 23=8 policies. The full table can choose different actions after histories (x,z) and (y,z), while the memoryless policy must use the same action for both because their final percept is z. This is a syntactic count over all histories; a fixed environment may make some histories unreachable, so distinct tables can behave identically there.

Question 2. The empty-history convention

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical problem

There are two percepts, three actions and a horizon of two percepts. How does permitting an action before any percept change the agent-function count?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Without an initial action, table entries correspond to 2+4=6 nonempty histories, so there are 36=729 functions. If an action is also assigned to the empty history, one additional entry appears. It can independently choose one of three actions, giving 37=2187. The factor is three, not a factor of two or an extra history at every depth. This convention does not change the environment's physical state count; it changes the domain on which the behavioural function is specified.

Question 3. One percept does not eliminate time dependence

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical problem

An agent always observes the same percept and chooses from four actions over five decisions. Count arbitrary history-based functions on these decision histories and stationary memoryless policies.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

There is exactly one history of each length, so the five decision histories are distinct by length even though every symbol is identical. Each can receive any of four actions, producing 45=1024 functions. A stationary memoryless policy sees only the current symbol, not its occurrence count, and must select the same action each time. It has four possibilities. A controller with a clock can implement a nonstationary sequence, but that clock is internal state and is not part of a stationary current-percept-only rule.

Question 4. Reachable histories versus all tables

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original conceptual and counting problem

Two percepts are syntactically possible, but a deterministic environment always emits X on both of two decisions regardless of action. With three actions, count full tables on nonempty histories through length two and distinct behaviours in this environment.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The full domain contains 2+4=6 histories and therefore 36=729 tables. Only X and XX are reachable. Behaviour in this environment is specified by the action on X and the action on XX, giving 32=9 behaviours. Each behaviour is implemented by 34=81 tables differing only at unreachable histories. The counts satisfy 9·81=729. Reachability is independent of action here by explicit assumption; in a general environment one must compute reachability under each policy before using this simplification.

Question 5. Contingent policy count

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical problem

A two-stage decision has two first actions, three possible observations after either first action, and four second actions after each observation. Count full deterministic contingent policies and fixed action sequences.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Choose the first action in two ways. For that chosen action, select one of four second actions separately for each of three possible observations, giving 43 continuations. There are 2·43=128 contingent policies. A fixed sequence ignores the observation, so it has only 2·4=8 possibilities. This counts executable policies from the given start, not a table assigning unused continuations after the first action that was not chosen. Such a larger table would contain behaviourally irrelevant entries and would have a different count.

Question 6. Counting a specified finite controller

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical problem

A deterministic Moore controller has two labelled internal states, three percepts and two actions. It updates state from the old internal state and current percept, then outputs the action assigned to the new state. Count syntactic controllers, including the initial internal state.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The update table has 2·3=6 entries, each selecting one of two internal states, giving 26 possibilities. The action table has two entries, each selecting one of two actions, giving 22 possibilities. The initial internal state has two choices. Multiply to obtain 2·26·22=512. This is a labelled syntactic count: isomorphic state renamings or unreachable internal states can implement the same behaviour. A Mealy controller whose output also depends directly on the percept has another signature and must be counted separately.

Question 7. Vacuum configurations and belief subsets

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical problem

A two-room vacuum has a labelled position and two independent dirt bits. Count physical states, nonempty belief subsets, and the physical states compatible with percept (L, clean).

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The physical count is 2·2·2=8. Every subset of these eight states is a syntactically possible set belief, so there are 28−1=255 nonempty subsets. The given percept fixes position L and dirt bit dL=0, leaving dR free. Exactly two states remain: (L,0,0) and (L,0,1). Neither 255 nor two is the physical state-space size. Moreover, not all 255 subsets must be reachable under the particular transition and sensor model.

Question 8. Exactly k dirty rooms

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical problem

A robot can occupy any of six labelled rooms, and exactly two rooms are dirty. Count configurations when occupation of a dirty room is allowed, and when the robot must occupy a clean room.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

With unrestricted location, choose the two dirty rooms in (62)=15 ways and then choose any of six locations, giving 90. Under the clean-location condition, each dirty-room choice leaves four allowed locations, giving 15·4=60. Equivalently, choose the robot's location first in six ways and select two dirty rooms among the other five: 6(52)=60. The equality checks the constraint count. Multiplying 6·26 would include dirt patterns with the wrong number of dirty rooms.

Question 9. Constraints can couple choices

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical problem

An elevator has ten possible stopped floors and one aggregate moving state. At a stopped floor its doors may be open or closed. While moving they must be closed. Count legal states and explain why this is not a complete route-planning state.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

There are 10·2=20 stopped states and one legal moving state, giving 21. The naive product 11·2=22 includes the forbidden moving-with-open-doors combination. For route planning, one aggregate moving state generally omits the direction and the segment or destination, so its next floor is not determined. The count is correct for the explicitly declared coarse status model, but it does not establish that the model is sufficient for predicting elevator movement.

Question 10. Labelled robots and collision exclusions

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical problem

Two labelled robots occupy distinct rooms among four, and each room has an independent dirt bit. Count states. When can the robots be treated as indistinguishable?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Choose the first robot's room in four ways and the second's in three, then choose four dirt bits in 24 ways. The count is 4·3·16=192. If exchanging robot labels preserves actions, dynamics, sensor roles and performance, unordered occupied-room sets have (42)=6 choices and the quotient count is 6·16=96. Different batteries, capacities or destinations can invalidate that symmetry. The smaller count is justified by a model invariance, not by the robots merely looking similar.

Question 11. Expected utility despite an unlucky outcome

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical problem

Safe pays 4 certainly. Risky pays 10 with probability 3/5 and −2 otherwise. Under utility equal to the numerical payoff, which action is rational? Does a realized −2 refute that answer?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Compute the risky expectation by weighting both outcomes: (3/5)10+(2/5)(−2)=6−4/5=26/5. Safe has expectation 4=20/5, so risky is better by 6/5. A realized loss of −2 has probability 2/5 under the model and is compatible with the optimal decision. To challenge the decision, one would need to challenge the probabilities, utilities, available alternatives or evaluation criterion. Judging the choice using future information the agent did not have confuses rationality with omniscience.

Expected utility and the realized outcome

The risky action has expectation 26/5; its negative branch remains possible.

A lower realized result does not retrospectively alter the available-information optimum.

Step 1 of 3

3510+25(-2)=265>4

Question 12. A threshold different from one half

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical problem

Action A pays 12 in H and −4 in L. Action B pays 5 in either state. Let P(H)=p. Derive the entire optimal-action set, including boundaries.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The expectations are EU(A)=12p−4(1−p)=16p−4 and EU(B)=5. Their difference is 16p−9. Thus B is uniquely optimal for 0≤p<9/16, both are optimal at p=9/16, and A is uniquely optimal for 9/16<p≤1. At p=0, A pays −4 and B pays 5; at p=1, A pays 12 and B pays 5, checking the inequality direction. Merely testing whether p exceeds one half would choose A incorrectly throughout (1/2,9/16).

The exact probability threshold

A = (12, −4), B = (5, 5); the threshold is 9/16, not 1/2.

The pointer moves along a fixed probability axis; the numerical checkpoint is exact.

Step 1 of 5

EU(A)-EU(B)=16p-9

Question 13. A negative coefficient reverses the inequality

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical problem

A pays (1,9) in states H,L, while B pays (4,4). Find when A is preferred, and explain the boundary case.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Here EU(A)=p+9(1−p)=9−8p and EU(B)=4. The comparison 9−8p≥4 becomes −8p≥−5. Dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality, giving p≤5/8. Both actions tie at 5/8; A is unique below it and B unique above it. The endpoint check p=1 gives A=1 and B=4, confirming that A cannot be the high-p action. The algebraic sign has a concrete interpretation: increasing H probability hurts A.

Question 14. Weak dominance and zero-probability states

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical problem

A pays (7,3) and B pays (7,1) in H,L. Is A always strictly better in expectation? Identify all ties.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

A is at least as good in both states and strictly better in L. The expectation difference is 2P(L)=2(1−p). It is positive for p<1, but equals zero when p=1. Thus weak statewise dominance implies no lower expectation, not unconditional strict preference. At p=1, L has no probability and its payoff difference contributes nothing. If a later observation assigns L positive posterior mass, the strict comparison can reappear.

Question 15. Positive affine utility transformation

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original proof problem

Prove that replacing outcome utility U by 3U−7 preserves expected-utility action rankings. Why does this proof not cover squaring arbitrary utility values?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

For each action, expectation is linear, so E[3U−7]=3E[U]−7. Subtract the transformed expectations of A and B: the constants cancel and the difference is 3(E[UA]−E[UB]). Multiplication by positive three preserves its sign and every tie. Squaring is nonlinear, so E[U2] is not generally (E[U])2; it also fails to be increasing over all real utilities. For instance utilities −2 and −1 reverse order after squaring. Even an increasing nonlinear transformation on a restricted domain can change lottery rankings.

Question 16. Increasing outcome transformations can reverse lotteries

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical problem

Lottery A pays 0 or 100 equally likely; B pays 40 certainly. Compare expected money and expected square-root utility.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Expected money is 50 for A and 40 for B, so a money-linear decision maker chooses A. With u(x)=x, A has expected utility (0+10)/2=5, while B has 40. Since 40>25, 40>5, so B is preferred. The square-root function is increasing on nonnegative outcomes, preserving their certain-outcome order, but it is not affine and changes risk tradeoffs. Neither preference is inconsistent with rationality once the corresponding utility is specified.

Question 17. Expected utility versus maximin

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical problem

A pays (8,−2), B pays (3,3), and P(H)=4/5. Compare the expected-utility and maximin choices.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The expectation of A is (4/5)8+(1/5)(−2)=6, whereas B has expectation 3. Expected utility selects A. The worst payoff of A is −2 and of B is 3, so maximin selects B. Maximin does not use the supplied prior; it protects against the worst state. The conflict is a difference in criterion, not a calculation error. Without probabilities or an alternative criterion, a payoff table alone does not select a unique rational action.

Question 18. Minimax regret is not maximin

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical problem

Payoffs in H,L are A= (10,0), B= (6,5), C= (0,8). Compute maximum regret and identify the minimax-regret action.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The best payoff in H is 10 and in L is 8. Subtract each payoff from the best in the same state. A has regrets (0,8), B has (4,3) and C has (10,0). Their maximum regrets are 8,4,10, so B uniquely minimizes worst regret. The worst payoffs are 0,5,0, so maximin happens to choose B here too, but for a different calculation. Regret must use statewise best payoffs; subtracting one global maximum 10 from both columns would create the wrong L regrets.

Question 19. An objective proxy rewards the wrong action

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical and conceptual problem

An agent can Clean, Announce or Stop. Clean removes one unit of dirt and costs 2; Announce changes no dirt and costs 0. A proposed reward is 3 per announcement. Over three actions, compare the reward-maximizing behaviour with maximizing dirt removed minus cost.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Under the proposed proxy, three announcements yield 9 and dominate any sequence using Clean or Stop, which do not earn announcement reward. The world may remain dirty throughout. Under the alternative score “dirt removed minus cost”, one Clean gives 1−2=−1, so with these numbers Stop gives the best score zero. This second criterion is also not a specification that prioritizes cleaning: its reward is too small to justify the cost. If cleaning is required, impose it as a goal/constraint or assign a consistent benefit. The analysis must inspect the actual numeric objective rather than assume its name expresses the desired behaviour.

Question 20. A finite penalty is not a hard constraint

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical problem

A safe delivery yields 20. An unsafe delivery yields 30−M. Find the penalty needed to prefer the safe action here, then explain why no fixed finite penalty handles arbitrarily large unsafe benefits.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Safe is at least as good if 20≥30−M, so M≥10; it is uniquely better if M>10. At M=10 the actions tie, so a policy may still choose unsafe unless the tie rule excludes it. If the unsafe benefit can be any B, its penalized value is B−M. For any finite M, choose B>20+M and unsafe wins. A hard safety constraint removes unsafe choices irrespective of reward magnitude. Finite penalties can enforce safety only with a justified bound and suitable tie handling.

Question 21. Known is independent of deterministic

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original conceptual problem

Classify a fair die with a known distribution and a door with an unknown but fixed code along the known/unknown and deterministic/stochastic axes. State the modelling assumptions.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The die model assigns probability 1/6 to each result under a roll. Its distribution is known, but the transition is stochastic. The door opens exactly when the entered code matches its fixed code. If the code is part of the physical state and the actuator is reliable, the transition is deterministic; the agent initially lacks the parameter. It is therefore unknown to that agent. A belief distribution over possible codes represents epistemic uncertainty and does not by itself make the fully specified door physics stochastic. Adding mechanical failure would change the transition model.

Question 22. Hidden determinism can produce predictive uncertainty

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical problem

A hidden bit Z is sampled once with P(Z=1)=3/4 and then remains fixed. The action Reveal deterministically emits Z. Is uncertainty about the next observation proof of a stochastic transition after Z is included in state?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

No. Conditional on the full state Z=0 or Z=1, Reveal has a unique observation and leaves the bit unchanged. The agent's predictive distribution is P(o=1)=3/4 because it does not know which fixed state is actual. Initial-state uncertainty produces a mixture of deterministic possibilities. If Reveal is repeated after the first result, the next result is certain under the model; treating each result as an independent Bernoulli draw would incorrectly allow the bit to change. The initial sampling can be stochastic while subsequent state transitions are deterministic.

Question 23. A static puzzle changes after action

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original conceptual problem

A sliding puzzle changes only when the agent moves a tile. It remains unchanged while the agent computes. Is it static? What changes if a score decreases once per second of thought?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The original task is static because no exogenous evolution occurs during deliberation. Its response to the agent's move is entirely compatible with static classification. If only the score decreases while the board remains fixed, the task is semidynamic: physical configuration is unchanged but performance depends on elapsed time. If elapsed time also makes moves illegal, represent time or deadlines in the state and describe that broader dynamics. The phrase “the environment ever changes” is too coarse to distinguish these cases.

Question 24. Independent inputs with coupled decisions

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original conceptual problem

A classifier receives independent images, but can request at most two expensive annotations in a session of ten images. Is annotation choice episodic?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

No. Requesting an annotation uses part of the shared budget and changes the available actions on future images. The input distribution can remain independent while the decision problem is sequential. A sufficient state includes the remaining annotation budget and, for a finite horizon, the number of images remaining when future opportunities depend on it. Without the shared budget and with additive independent per-image losses, separate classification decisions could be episodic. Independence of observations is not independence of action consequences.

Question 25. Discrete does not mean finite

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original conceptual and counting problem

A sensor reports a nonnegative integer counter, and actions are Increment or Stop. Time advances in discrete steps. Is this a finite-state task? How does a cap at 20 change the answer?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The uncapped state set {0,1,2,…} is countably infinite and discrete. Two actions and discrete time do not make the state set finite. With a hard cap at 20 and Increment defined to leave 20 unchanged, the counter has exactly 21 states. A stop/termination flag would add states if retained separately; it should not be silently included or excluded. In a finite horizon H from zero, only counters up to H may be reachable even in the uncapped physical model.

Question 26. Single controller, several bodies

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original conceptual problem

One central program chooses joint actions for three robots. An opposing team has its own program. Is the central program's task necessarily single-agent because it controls all three robots?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

It can treat its own three robots as one decision maker whose action is a triple. The independently controlled opposing team still creates a multi-agent interaction. The number of physical robots does not determine the number of strategic decision makers. If each robot has four possible commands and every joint combination is legal, the central action set has 43=64 elements. Collision or communication constraints can remove combinations. A deterministic transition given both teams' joint commands does not remove uncertainty about the opponent's choice.

Question 27. Partial observability without a memory advantage

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original proof and counterexample problem

Two hidden states produce the same percept. In both states action A gives utility 5 and action B gives utility 1. Prove that a memoryless policy is rational for any belief over the two states.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Let the first state's probability be p. Then EU(A)=5p+5(1−p)=5 and EU(B)=p+(1−p)=1. A is uniquely optimal for all p∈[0,1]. The sensor is partially informative because it cannot distinguish the states, yet that distinction is irrelevant to the optimal choice. Memory might estimate p more accurately, but no p changes the maximizing action. This counterexample refutes the universal claim that every partially observable task requires memory for rational action.

Hidden states can share the same best action

Partial observability does not force a loss when every hidden state has the same maximizing action.

State uncertainty remains, but it does not change this decision.

Step 1 of 3

5p+5(1-p)=5

Question 28. Aliased histories with incompatible optima

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original proof problem

The same current percept occurs after histories h1,h2. At h1, utilities of A,B are (10,0); at h2, they are (0,10). Can any current-percept-only deterministic or randomized rule be optimal at both histories?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

A deterministic rule outputs one action for that percept. A is uniquely optimal at the first history and B at the second, so neither fixed choice works at both. Let a randomized rule choose A with probability q. Its utility is 10q at h1 and 10(1−q) at h2. To reach the optimum ten at the first requires q=1, while at the second requires q=0. These conditions are incompatible. At least two distinguishable internal conditions, or an additional observation, are necessary to implement both optimal choices.

Identical percept, incompatible history-dependent optima

Both histories end with the same sensor symbol, but the uniquely correct actions differ.

Store a key bit or obtain another observation; changing the rule alone cannot recover omitted information.

{Open}∩{Find key}=∅

Question 29. Overlapping optimal-action sets

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical problem

Three histories share one percept. Their maximizing sets are {A,B}, {B,C} and {B,D}. Does a rational deterministic reflex rule exist? What if the third set becomes {A,D}?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Intersect the three sets. In the first case, the only common action is B, so selecting B is optimal at every history despite their different states. After changing the third set, the intersection of the first two remains {B}, but B is absent from {A,D}; the full intersection is empty. Pairwise considerations are not a substitute for the common intersection over all relevant histories. The result presupposes that these maximizing sets correctly incorporate the same task objective and continuation horizon.

Question 30. Goal achievement versus maintenance

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original conceptual problem

A trajectory visits Safe, Collision, Destination. Does it satisfy “eventually reach Destination” and “never enter Collision”? Can a terminal test using only the final location distinguish it from Safe, Destination?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The first trajectory reaches Destination and satisfies the achievement goal. It violates the maintenance requirement because it visited Collision. Both trajectories have the same final location, so a terminal predicate depending only on that location cannot distinguish their safety histories. Retain an “ever collided” bit or evaluate the entire trajectory. If collisions are absorbing and prevent reaching Destination, the task changes; that additional transition assumption must be stated rather than inferred from the word collision.

Question 31. A compiled reflex policy can implement planning

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original conceptual problem

A finite fully observed task has an optimal stationary policy computed offline. At runtime a table maps each observed state directly to its stored optimal action. Is runtime lookahead necessary for rationality?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

No. If the model, objective and sufficient state remain as assumed, the table implements the computed optimal policy directly. Its runtime mechanism is a state-conditioned response, although planning was used to construct it. Rationality concerns the chosen action under the task criterion, not whether the program visibly simulates futures every time. If the objective is finite-horizon and the optimal policy depends on time remaining, include time in the table key. An outdated model or incomplete percept can invalidate the offline policy's guarantee.

Question 32. Model-based does not mean online planning

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original conceptual problem

A vacuum remembers whether each room has been verified clean, updates those bits from observations and applies fixed rules to move, clean or stop. Explain why it can be model-based and reflex at the same time.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

It is model-based because its persistent summary uses assumptions about cleaning, movement and whether dirt can recur. It is reflex in the architectural sense that action selection applies a rule to the updated internal condition rather than searching future action sequences at runtime. Memory and lookahead are separate design dimensions. If cleaning is unreliable, setting a clean bit from the command alone is unjustified; the controller must verify the result or represent uncertainty. Thus the model label requires actual transition/observation assumptions, not merely storing a variable.

Question 33. Learning without physical stochasticity

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original conceptual problem

A robot explores a fixed deterministic maze whose map is initially unknown. Another robot navigates a stochastic maze with all transition probabilities supplied. Which one must learn a transition model?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The first may need to acquire unknown map information to navigate effectively, although a particular easy goal could be achievable without learning the whole map. Determinism does not supply the missing map. The second already has its transition model; stochasticity alone does not require estimating it from experience. It can plan using the supplied probabilities. Both might learn useful policies or computational shortcuts, but those are separate tasks. “Must learn” needs a performance requirement and remaining opportunities, not only an environment label.

Question 34. Exploration can cost more than it is worth

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical problem

An experiment costs 5 utility units. Even with perfect information, all remaining action choices could improve expected utility by at most 2. Is the experiment rational if it has no other benefit?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The information-induced improvement is bounded above by 2, and the cost is 5. Thus the net gain is at most 2−5=−3. Not experimenting weakly improves utility by at least three relative to this experiment under the assumptions. Unknown parameters do not create an unconditional obligation to explore. If the experiment also produces direct reward or changes future available actions, include those effects and recompute the bound; the conclusion relies on their explicit exclusion.

Question 35. Computation has an opportunity cost

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical problem

A fast program selects an action worth 8 in expectation. A slower program selects an action worth 10, but delay costs 3. Compare net performance and give the general condition for using the slower computation.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The fast program's net utility is 8. The slow program's net utility is 10−3=7, so the fast program is better by one. In general let the expected improvement from extra computation be Δ and its total utility cost be c. Extra computation is worthwhile only if Δ>c, with a tie at equality. This comparison must include environmental change during thought, computation cost and any deadline effects. Comparing only the selected action quality would omit part of the task performance.

Question 36. Current position omits a key

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original state-modelling problem

At room X, action Open reaches the goal only if a key was collected earlier. Two histories end at X, one with a key and one without. Show why position alone is not a sufficient state and give a sufficient augmentation for this rule.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Both histories map to the same position X, yet the action's legality or successor differs depending on the key. Therefore no single transition T(X,Open) captures both histories exactly. Use state (x,k) with a key bit k∈{0,1}, assuming all other future-relevant information is already encoded in x. The two histories become (X,1) and (X,0) and their different action outcomes are well-defined. This is a concrete violation of the Markov/sufficiency requirement, not merely a claim that history is generally useful.

A key bit repairs an invalid state abstraction

At the same position X, Open has different legality depending on key possession.

A missing key is a missing precondition, not a different arrow label on the same exact abstract edge.

Question 37. Time can matter in stationary physics

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical problem

A project action pays −1 now and 5 at the following decision. A safe action pays 2 now and terminates. With undiscounted finite-horizon reward, compare the choices when one versus two decisions remain.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

With one decision remaining, the project's later reward lies outside the horizon, so its return is −1 and safe gives 2; safe wins. With two decisions remaining and the promised later reward guaranteed, project returns −1+5=4, exceeding safe's 2. The physical transition rule did not change, but the optimal action depends on remaining horizon. A stationary position-only policy cannot implement both choices at the same physical state. Use a time-indexed policy or augment state with the remaining decision count.

Question 38. Distinct beliefs with identical support

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical problem

Hidden states are H,L and utilities are A= (12,−4), B= (5,5). Compare beliefs P(H)=1/4 and P(H)=3/4. Can a support set alone encode the optimal choice?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Both beliefs have support {H,L} because each state has positive probability. At p=1/4, EU(A)=0 and B=5, so choose B. At p=3/4, EU(A)=8 and B=5, so choose A. The common support set records possibility but not relative weight. A worst-case or guaranteed-goal task might use set beliefs appropriately, but an expected-utility task generally requires probabilities or another sufficient statistic retaining the decision-relevant weights.

Question 39. Bayesian conditioning must include the prior

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical problem

Let P(H)=3/10, P(+∣H)=4/5 and P(+∣L)=1/5. Compute the positive-signal probability and the posterior of H. Explain why 4/5 is not the posterior.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The joint positive masses are (3/10)(4/5)=12/50 in H and (7/10)(1/5)=7/50 in L. Their sum is 19/50. Normalize the H mass: P(H∣+)=(12/50)/(19/50)=12/19. The likelihood 4/5 conditions on H and asks how often the signal is positive; the posterior conditions on a positive signal and asks how often H is true. These are different conditional probabilities, with the prior determining how much L contributes to observed positives.

Bayes update: joint mass before normalization

Prior H=3/10; positive likelihoods are 4/5 and 1/5. Normalize joint mass, not likelihood alone.

The bar lengths represent exact probabilities; numerical values use rational arithmetic.

Question 40. The negative observation matters too

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original mathematical problem

Under the binary sensor in Question 39, derive the negative-signal probability and posterior, then verify that posterior averaging recovers the prior.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Negative likelihoods are 1/5 in H and 4/5 in L. The H negative mass is 3/50, the L negative mass is 28/50, so P(−)=31/50 and P(H∣−)=3/31. Average the posteriors with their signal probabilities: (19/50)(12/19)+(31/50)(3/31)=12/50+3/50=15/50=3/10. This is total probability applied to H. Averaging 12/19 and 3/31 equally would be wrong because the signal outcomes are not equally likely.

Prior H=3/10; positive likelihoods are 4/5 and 1/5. Normalize joint mass, not likelihood alone.
